platforms.name: Claude Enterprise (Anthropic) — two new dated entries, Aug 18 and Aug 19
details: **Browser use tool (`browser_toolset_20260801`), Aug 19.** A client toolset for driving a browser the *application* hosts, working inside a viewport rather than a whole desktop. Reads the page's **accessibility tree** via `read_page`, returning stable element references (`[ref_1]`…) that Claude acts on by reference instead of coordinates; `find` locates elements from natural-language descriptions and `get_page_text` extracts visible text. Members include `navigate` (with `back`/`forward`/`reload`), the full pointer and keyboard set, `form_input`, `screenshot`, `zoom`, and tab management (`new_tab`, `list_tabs`, `switch_tab`, `close_tab`). Four members are **optional and disabled by default**: `javascript_exec`, `file_upload`, `read_console`, `read_network`. `file_upload` sets files on `<input type="file">` from either executor filesystem `paths` or application-staged `document_ids`. The application must report tab inventory through `browser_state` blocks and downloads through `state_changes`. Anthropic's guidance: run the browser in a dedicated container with no credentials, enforce domain allowlisting at the network layer, refuse `javascript:`/`file:`/`data:`/`chrome:` schemes, sanitize page-supplied URLs and titles, and require human confirmation for consequential actions. Source: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/browser-use-tool

**Computer use tool GA (`computer_toolset_20260801`), Aug 19.** No beta header; adds **batch actions** (several actions in one turn), `zoom` enabled by default, and **per-member configuration through `configs`**. Earlier beta versions remain available, and upgrading changes the request shape. Source: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/computer-use-tool

**Agent Skills and the Skills API (`/v1/skills`) GA, Aug 19.** The `skills-2025-10-02` beta header is no longer required, including on Messages API requests that load Skills through the `container` parameter. Source: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/skills-guide

**Domain restrictions for Managed Agents' `web_search` and `web_fetch`, Aug 19.** `allowed_domains` / `blocked_domains` set per-tool in the `agent_toolset_20260401` `configs` array; `web_fetch` also takes `max_content_tokens`, `web_search` takes `user_location`. Each `configs` entry is keyed by `name` and typed by an optional `type`. Source: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/tools#restrict-web-search-and-web-fetch-domains

**Memory stores attachable to self-hosted sandboxes, Aug 19.** The Python, TypeScript and Go SDK workers download each attached store into the customer's own sandbox at its `mount_path` and **sync the agent's changes back**. platforms.name: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore — five new August entries
details: **Payments: x402 `upto` scheme and Machine Payments Protocol (MPP).** The `upto` scheme **pays a metered amount up to a ceiling and settles through the Permit2 contract**, in addition to the existing `exact` scheme. MPP is an HTTP-native standard using the standard authentication-challenge flow: a merchant returns `WWW-Authenticate: Payment` in a `402 Payment Required`, the agent forwards the challenge verbatim to `ProcessPayment` with `paymentType=MPP`, and **AgentCore parses the challenge, checks the session budget, signs with the wallet, and returns a ready-to-send credential** that the caller replays in an `Authorization` header. Supports `evm`, `tempo` and `solana` payment methods, with provider support varying by connector type. Source: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/payments-process-payment.html

**Payments: Quick create for Coinbase payment connectors.** AgentCore payments **provisions your Coinbase CDP credentials for you** — you authorize through Coinbase in a browser and the service creates the payment credential provider on your behalf. No API keys are generated or pasted by a human. Coinbase only; Stripe (Privy) still uses supplied credentials. Source: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/payments-create-manager.html

**Evaluations: Skill evaluators.** Two built-in tool-level evaluators — `Builtin.SkillSelectionAccuracy` (did the loaded skill fit the task, given the catalog) and `Builtin.SkillInstructionFollowing` (a five-point rating of how fully the agent followed the skill's prescribed steps). One result per skill invocation, anchored to the tool-call span that loaded the skill. Custom `TOOL_CALL` evaluators can read the same signals through the `invoked_skill`, `skill_content`, `available_skills` and `user_message` placeholders. Source: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/skill-evaluators.html

**Evaluations: Third-party evaluators.** Evaluators from the **DeepEval and AutoEval** open-source libraries, either managed (selected by ID and run by AWS on a model it operates) or derived (the library's logic run on the customer's own model and inference). Both are discoverable through `ListEvaluators` alongside built-in and custom evaluators. Source: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/third-party-evaluators.html
*(Not reported: Coinbase wallet usage billed through AWS Marketplace — billing plumbing; memory/policy/harness in GovCloud (US-West) — region expansion.)*

platforms.name: Amazon Bedrock — three new entries, and a reversal of last week's guidance
details: **`bedrock-runtime` now serves the Anthropic and OpenAI API shapes, and is again the recommended endpoint (Aug 15 and Aug 19).** Endpoint guidance across the User Guide was rewritten to **recommend `bedrock-runtime` for new applications, including for OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible workloads** — the direct opposite of the guidance captured on 2026-08-14. Concretely: Anthropic Messages API samples now target `https://bedrock-runtime.{region}.amazonaws.com/anthropic`, and the `OPENAI_BASE_URL` on **49 non-Anthropic model cards** (OpenAI, Mistral, DeepSeek, Google, Meta, Qwen, MiniMax, Moonshot, Z.AI, Writer, xAI, NVIDIA) was repointed from the `bedrock-mantle` `/v1` route to **`https://bedrock-runtime.{region}.amazonaws.com/openai/v1`**. `bedrock-mantle` "continues to be fully supported" and remains the only host for mantle-only features — **Web Search, Projects, Workspaces, Chat Completions on mantle, and the mantle Responses API**. Also added: **Daybreak Red: GPT-5.6 Cyber and Daybreak Blue: GPT-5.6 Sol to the Models at a glance table**. Source: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/endpoints.html

**Bedrock Projects and Workspaces.** Surfaced by the endpoint work above; never inventoried by this monitor. A **Project** (OpenAI-compatible) and a **Workspace** (Anthropic-compatible) are **the same underlying resource**, managed by the **Projects API** at `POST/GET https://bedrock-mantle.{region}.api.aws/v1/organization/projects`, returning `arn:aws:bedrock-mantle:…:project/proj_…`. They differ only in the header used to bind inference to them: `OpenAI-Project: {project-id}` versus `anthropic-workspace: {project-id}`. Each is an **IAM resource** with tags, a `status`, and an archive lifecycle; every account has a **default workspace/project** that all inference is attributed to unless another is named. Source: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/workspaces.html

**AgentCore Memory integration for Bedrock agentic retrieval (Aug 14).** Agentic retrieval on fully managed Bedrock knowledge bases now integrates with **AgentCore Memory** through a `memoryConfiguration` field on **`AgenticRetrieveStream`**. You can restore an earlier session from short-term memory, let the agent retrieve records from long-term memory, or both. Source: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-test-agentic-retrieve.html

findings.title: Anthropic shipped a browser-driving toolset that reads the accessibility tree and can be flagged into JavaScript execution, console and network capture
findings.description: `browser_toolset_20260801` is a new client toolset that drives a browser the customer's own application hosts, working inside a viewport rather than a whole desktop. Its reading model is the finding's core: `read_page` returns the page's **accessibility tree** as text with stable element references (`[ref_1]`, `[ref_2]`…) and Claude then acts **by reference** rather than by coordinate, with `find` resolving elements from natural-language descriptions and `get_page_text` extracting visible text. That makes the agent's interaction with a page semantic and reliable in a way screenshot-and-click never was, which raises the ceiling on what a prompt injection embedded in a page can actually accomplish. **Anthropic's own documentation leads with that risk** — it instructs implementers to treat every page-supplied string (titles, URLs, text) as untrusted, sanitize before returning it to Claude, refuse `javascript:`/`file:`/`data:`/`chrome:` schemes in the navigate handler, enforce domain allowlisting **at the network layer**, run the browser in a dedicated container with no credentials, and require human confirmation for purchases, account modifications and messaging. Four members are optional and off by default, and each one is a distinct escalation an implementer can silently enable: **`javascript_exec`** runs arbitrary JavaScript in page context, **`read_console`** and **`read_network`** expose logs and requests that routinely carry tokens and secrets (Anthropic explicitly says to redact before enabling them), and **`file_upload`** sets files on `<input type="file">` from either executor filesystem `paths` or application-staged `document_ids` — with the warning that a malicious page could otherwise direct uploads of any accessible file. AIRT should build page-hosted injection tests against reference-based interaction specifically, and test whether a hostile page can induce navigation to a non-HTTP scheme, an unapproved consequential action, or a `file_upload` outside its intended directory. AISPM should discover which applications enable this toolset and, per deployment, which optional members are turned on, treating `javascript_exec` and `file_upload` as privileged configuration; AIDR should ingest `browser_state` tab inventories and `state_changes` download events as agent activity, since a download reported there is data leaving a page and landing on the executor

findings.title: The ChatGPT Mac app can now read and send iMessage, SMS and RCS, and requires Full Disk Access to do it
findings.description: OpenAI shipped an **Apple Messages plugin** that lets ChatGPT search a user's entire Messages history, summarize past conversations, draft replies, and **send messages** through Messages. It covers **iMessage, SMS and RCS**, so it reaches SMS-delivered content including one-time passcodes and MFA codes. The permission requirement is the finding: the integration needs **Full Disk Access** in macOS System Settings, plus access to contact names and automation tooling — a grant that extends far beyond Messages and that endpoint policy at most enterprises treats as high-privilege. Two more properties matter for coverage. First, the **send-approval model degrades by design**: sends require user approval by default, but users can choose **"Always allow sending to this chat"**, which OpenAI itself warns removes the final review before ChatGPT sends on the user's behalf — so a per-conversation toggle silently converts a human-in-the-loop control into autonomous outbound messaging. Second, availability is **narrower than "the ChatGPT desktop app"**: the plugin ships only in the **Apple Silicon (arm64)** build and does nothing on Intel Macs, the web, mobile, Codex CLI or the IDE extension — reinforcing that per-OS-and-architecture feature modelling is now required rather than optional. It is available on all plans and installed from Plugins > Public, and works from **both ChatGPT Work and Codex**, so it is reachable from a coding agent as well as the chat client. ENDPOINT should detect the plugin's installed and enabled state per device, detect the Full Disk Access grant to the ChatGPT app as a distinct high-risk condition, and inventory which conversations have persistent send approval; AIDR should treat agent-originated messages as an outbound data-flow channel; AIRT should test whether content arriving in a message thread can steer the agent into sending on the user's behalf where persistent approval is already granted

findings.title: Codex now connects to GitLab with `@codex` triggers on issues and merge requests and automatic reviews
findings.description: OpenAI extended Codex cloud beyond GitHub. You can now **connect GitLab projects**, create cloud environments against them, **trigger tasks by mentioning `@codex` on issues and merge requests**, and **enable automatic reviews**. This is a new code-host integration surface, not a variation on an existing one, and it matters for three reasons. It is a **second source-control identity to discover and scope**: setup covers webhook permissions, so Codex holds a standing credential and webhook grant against GitLab projects, and the effective blast radius is whatever that credential can read and write across connected projects. It **moves the trigger boundary out of the developer's hands**: with `@codex` mentions and automatic reviews enabled, an agent task can be started by anyone who can comment on an issue or open a merge request — including, on projects that accept outside contributions, someone who is not an employee. And it **extends the injection path**: issue and merge-request bodies are attacker-influenceable text that now reaches an agent with repository access, the same pattern Zenity should already be testing on the GitHub side. Note also that self-hosted GitLab remains reachable through the GitLab MCP server as a separate path, so a customer may have both a first-party Codex-GitLab connection and an MCP-mediated one. AISPM should discover Codex-to-GitLab connections, resolve the authenticating identity and its project scopes, enumerate which projects have automatic reviews enabled, and flag connections on projects that accept external contributions; AIRT should test `@codex` mention-triggered injection from issue and merge-request content

findings.title: Copilot Studio agents can now take an MCP server or a workflow as a tool on the GitHub Copilot harness
findings.description: The July 2026 Copilot Studio release adds the ability to attach a **workflow** or an **MCP server** as a tool to agents built on the **GitHub Copilot harness** — the new orchestration runtime that went production-ready preview in June. Both are new tool types on a new harness, which means the tool-attachment surface Zenity inventories for Copilot Studio is no longer complete. The MCP case is the more consequential: an MCP server attached as a tool brings an external, independently-operated endpoint into the agent's capability set, with its own tool list, its own authentication, and its own change cadence that no Copilot Studio review gate observes after attachment. The workflow case is a **privilege-composition** problem — a workflow is a multistep automated process that may itself hold connections and credentials, so attaching one grants the agent the workflow's reach rather than just a single action, and the agent's effective permissions become the union of its own and every attached workflow's. This lands on a platform where the harness itself is new, so agents on the GitHub Copilot harness should be treated as a distinct inventory class from standard-harness agents: they alone can hold MCP servers, workflows, skills, memory, Microsoft IQ and Foundry IQ connections, and file attachments. AISPM should enumerate agents by harness, discover attached MCP servers and resolve each to its endpoint, transport, authentication and advertised tool list, expand attached workflows to the connections and credentials they carry, and flag agents whose effective permissions grow through workflow attachment rather than direct grant. AIRT should test whether an attached MCP server's tool descriptions can inject instructions into the agent

findings.title: AgentCore agents can now settle open-ended, metered payments autonomously via the Machine Payments Protocol and the x402 `upto` scheme
findings.description: AgentCore payments added two payment modes that move agents from fixed-price transactions to open-ended commercial commitments. The **x402 `upto` scheme** "pays a metered amount up to a ceiling and settles through the Permit2 contract" — meaning the agent authorizes a range rather than an amount, and the final figure is determined by the counterparty's metering, not by the agent's own decision at authorization time. The **Machine Payments Protocol** is the larger change: a merchant returns a `WWW-Authenticate: Payment` challenge in a `402 Payment Required` response, the agent **forwards that challenge verbatim** to `ProcessPayment` with `paymentType=MPP`, and AgentCore **parses the challenge, checks the session budget, signs with the wallet, and returns a ready-to-send credential** which the caller replays in an `Authorization` header. Two things follow. First, **an untrusted party's HTTP response is the input that drives a wallet signature** — the challenge is merchant-supplied and forwarded unmodified, so the integrity of the payment depends on AgentCore's parsing and on the session budget being the only real ceiling. Second, the **session budget becomes the primary financial control**, which makes budget configuration a posture attribute of the first order rather than an operational setting. MPP supports the `evm`, `tempo` and `solana` payment methods with provider support varying by connector, so settlement can land on multiple chains from one agent. AIRT should test whether a manipulated or malicious `402` challenge can induce an over-payment, a payment to an unintended recipient, or a signature outside the intended scheme, and should probe the boundary between the `upto` ceiling and the session budget. AISPM should inventory payment managers, connectors, payment instruments and wallets as financial entities, record each session's configured budget and flag unbudgeted or high-ceiling sessions, and enumerate which agents hold payment capability at all; AIDR should treat `ProcessPayment` calls as a high-severity activity type with the counterparty, scheme and amount as required fields

findings.title: AWS moved the OpenAI and Anthropic API shapes onto `bedrock-runtime` and reversed last week's endpoint recommendation — endpoint no longer predicts wire format
findings.description: On August 15 and 19 AWS rewrote endpoint guidance across the Bedrock User Guide to **recommend `bedrock-runtime` for new applications, including for OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible workloads** — the direct reversal of the guidance this monitor captured on 2026-08-14, which recommended `bedrock-mantle`. The substantive part is not the recommendation but the **routing change underneath it**. Anthropic Messages API samples now target `https://bedrock-runtime.{region}.amazonaws.com/anthropic`, and the `OPENAI_BASE_URL` on **49 non-Anthropic model cards** (OpenAI, Mistral, DeepSeek, Google, Meta, Qwen, MiniMax, Moonshot AI, Z.AI, Writer, xAI, NVIDIA) was repointed from the mantle `/v1` route to **`https://bedrock-runtime.{region}.amazonaws.com/openai/v1`**. The consequence for detection is direct and immediate: **both Bedrock endpoints now serve foreign API shapes**, so a parser selected by hostname will mis-handle traffic, and last week's coverage recommendation — add OpenAI Responses, Chat Completions and Anthropic Messages parsers *for the mantle endpoint* — is now insufficient rather than wrong. Those shapes must be handled on `bedrock-runtime`'s `/anthropic` and `/openai/v1` routes too, and the authentication differs by route (a short-term bearer token from `aws-bedrock-token-generator` on one path, SigV4 via `AnthropicBedrock` on another). `bedrock-mantle` "continues to be fully supported" and remains the **only** host for mantle-only features — **Web Search, Projects, Workspaces, Chat Completions on mantle, and the mantle Responses API** — so neither endpoint can be dropped from coverage. AIDR should key parser selection on the **route path**, not the hostname, and cover `/anthropic`, `/openai/v1` and the mantle `/v1` routes; AISPM should re-inventory which endpoints and routes each workload actually reaches, since AWS's reversal means new applications built this week will look different from ones built last week

findings.title: Gemini Enterprise took customer-hosted A2UI/A2A agent registration to GA, letting external agents render their own UI inside the tenant
findings.description: Registering agents that use the **Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol** together with **Agent to UI (A2UI)** is now generally available, with **A2UI v0.9** adding Material Design components alongside v0.8. The architecture is what makes this a first-order inventory problem: the agent is **hosted and maintained by the customer or a third party, not by Google**, must be network-reachable by Gemini Enterprise for A2A communication, and is registered by a **Gemini Enterprise administrator** through the Cloud console or the **REST API** — after which it becomes available to users inside a Gemini Enterprise app. So a registered A2UI agent is an entity whose code, model, tools and data handling live entirely outside the platform Zenity is monitoring, while its output is rendered to users inside the trusted enterprise surface. A2UI compounds that: the external agent supplies **interface components**, not merely text, so it controls what the user sees and interacts with inside Gemini Enterprise — buttons, forms and inputs defined by a remote party. That is a phishing and consent-manipulation surface that a text-only agent does not have, and the v0.8-to-v0.9 span means two component protocols must be reasoned about. AISPM should discover registered A2A/A2UI agents through the REST API, record each agent's endpoint, owner, hosting location, A2UI version and declared capabilities, distinguish externally-hosted agents from Google-hosted ones as a distinct risk class, and flag agents registered outside a review process; AIRT should test whether an A2UI-supplied component can misrepresent a consequential action or harvest input, and whether A2A responses from a registered agent are treated as trusted instruction by the orchestrator

findings.title: Cursor now hosts source code — Origin is a git forge with bidirectional GitHub sync
findings.description: Cursor has shipped **Origin**, "Cursor's git forge for storing and sharing code" (early beta), moving a watching-tier IDE vendor into the code-hosting business. It supports repository creation, standard git operations, code browsing and search at `cursor.com/codebase`, and pull-request review and merge. Existing projects arrive by **GitHub mirroring**, and PRs on synced repos **sync bidirectionally** — a comment in Cursor posts to GitHub, and a reply on GitHub appears in Cursor within seconds. It integrates with **Vercel, Depot and Buildkite** for deployment and CI/CD, and with Cursor's own automations and cloud agents, plus an Origin CLI. This crosses the threshold for a watching-tier report because it is not an agent feature — it is a **new location where the customer's source code lives**, outside the sanctioned SCM, populated by a mirror that most organizations will not have approved as a code destination. Three specifics are worth capturing. The **bidirectional PR sync** means code review moves off the governed platform: an approval or comment recorded in Cursor is authoritative on GitHub, so branch-protection and review-audit assumptions anchored to GitHub no longer hold. The **CI/CD integrations** mean an Origin-hosted repo can reach deployment infrastructure directly. And the **privacy-mode interaction is a real control**: Origin requires Privacy Mode and "teams on legacy privacy mode cannot enable Origin", so whether a team switched modes to adopt it is a discoverable posture signal. Available on Pro, Teams and Enterprise. AISPM should detect Origin-hosted and Origin-mirrored repositories as a code location outside sanctioned SCM, resolve which namespaces are claimed and who holds repository access, and flag repositories whose PR review path runs through Cursor; ENDPOINT should detect Origin CLI installation on developer machines

findings.title: Anthropic Agent Skills and the Skills API went GA, making a skill an enumerable first-class API resource
findings.description: Agent Skills and the **Skills API (`/v1/skills`)** are now generally available on the Claude API, with the `skills-2025-10-02` beta header no longer required — including on Messages API requests that load Skills through the **`container`** parameter. The governance significance is that a skill has graduated from a beta-gated experiment to a durable, addressable resource with its own CRUD endpoint, which means two things at once. It is now a **discoverable inventory entity type**: `/v1/skills` gives Zenity a direct API path to enumerate every skill in an organization, its content and its metadata, without inferring skills from transcripts. And it is now **broadly reachable**: removing the beta header removes the friction that limited adoption, so skill counts should be expected to grow, and skills loaded through the `container` parameter attach to a session at runtime rather than being fixed in an agent's definition. A skill is instruction text that becomes part of the agent's operating context, so it is both a privilege-shaping object and an injection surface — and this GA lands in the same week that AgentCore shipped skill evaluators and Copilot Studio and Gemini Enterprise both expanded their own skill features, so "skill" is converging into a cross-platform entity type that Zenity should model once and map per platform. Note the cross-reference to a known blind spot: Anthropic's Compliance API transcripts include skill content only *when the client sends it*, so `/v1/skills` is the authoritative source and transcripts are not. AISPM should enumerate skills through `/v1/skills` as an inventory entity with owner, content and attachment points, inspect skill bodies for embedded credentials and for instructions that widen tool use, and reconcile skills observed at runtime through `container` against the registered set; AIRT should treat skill content as a persistent injection vector

findings.title: Copilot Studio now creates an Entra Agent ID for every new agent and has removed the environment-level opt-out
findings.description: As of July 2026, "Copilot Studio automatically creates a Microsoft Entra Agent ID for every new agent, and **you can no longer opt out at the environment level**." This completes a three-stage rollout — preview opt-in in November 2025, default-on in May 2026, now mandatory — and it is unusual among this report's findings in being **net-positive for discovery**: every new Copilot Studio agent is now guaranteed to exist as an addressable directory principal, so the Entra agent registry becomes a complete enumeration of new agents rather than a partial one, and Conditional Access, connector permission scoping and DLP can be applied per agent. Two caveats define the coverage work. First, **"every new agent" is not "every agent"**: agents created before the mandate in environments that had opted out will still lack an Agent ID, so a population of identity-less legacy agents persists and is exactly the set that a registry-based inventory will miss. That mirrors the `instance_identity`-null legacy-agent pattern already documented on the Foundry side, and the two should be reconciled with the same logic. Second, the removal of the opt-out means an **identity is created whether or not the maker or the tenant wanted one**, so agent-identity growth is now automatic and the count of Entra agent principals will rise with every agent built — making unused, orphaned and ownerless agent identities a maintenance problem that will grow on its own. AISPM should treat the Entra agent registry as authoritative for post-July Copilot Studio agents, separately enumerate pre-mandate agents lacking an Agent ID as a known-incomplete population, and reconcile both against Copilot Studio's own agent inventory schema so identity-less agents are visible rather than absent

findings.title: Bedrock Projects and Workspaces are an uninventoried control-plane isolation boundary managed by a Projects API
findings.description: Surfaced by the endpoint-guidance rewrite and never covered by this monitor, **Projects** (OpenAI-compatible) and **Workspaces** (Anthropic-compatible) are **the same underlying resource** under two names, managed by a single **Projects API** at `https://bedrock-mantle.{region}.api.aws/v1/organization/projects` and returning ARNs of the form `arn:aws:bedrock-mantle:…:project/proj_…`. They differ only in the header that binds inference to them — **`OpenAI-Project: {project-id}`** versus **`anthropic-workspace: {project-id}`**. Each carries a `name`, a `status`, AWS **tags**, an archive lifecycle, and is addressable **as a resource in IAM policies**, so a project is simultaneously an access-control boundary, a cost-allocation unit and an observability scope. Three points for coverage. This is a **new AWS entity type** with its own CRUD API that Zenity's Bedrock discovery does not enumerate, and AWS's recommended structure — one project per application per environment — means a mature customer will have many of them describing the real shape of their AI estate. The **header-based binding** means the project an inference request is attributed to is asserted **by the caller at request time**, not derived from the credential, so an inventory built only from control-plane state will not tell you which project traffic actually claimed. And **every account has a default project/workspace that all inference lands in unless another is named** — traffic resolving to the default is a strong signal of a workload that was never deliberately scoped, the same posture finding as Anthropic's Default Workspace. Note the naming collision worth guarding against: a Bedrock Workspace is not an Anthropic workspace, and `anthropic-workspace` here carries an AWS `proj_` ID. AISPM should enumerate projects through the Projects API, record tags, IAM policies and archive state, correlate the `OpenAI-Project` and `anthropic-workspace` headers observed in traffic against the enumerated set, and flag production inference attributed to the default project

findings.title: AgentCore skill evaluators confirm skills are a catalog-backed AgentCore entity and expose per-invocation skill signals
findings.description: AgentCore Evaluations added two built-in **tool-level** evaluators for agents that use skills: **`Builtin.SkillSelectionAccuracy`**, which judges whether the skill the agent loaded fits the task **given the catalog of available skills**, and **`Builtin.SkillInstructionFollowing`**, which rates on five points how fully the agent followed the loaded skill's prescribed steps. Results are produced **one per skill invocation** and **anchored to the tool-call span that loaded the skill**, and they work with on-demand, batch and online evaluations. Two things make this reportable beyond the evaluators themselves. It **confirms the shape of skills on AgentCore**: there is a catalog of available skills, a skill is *loaded* at runtime through a tool call, and a skill has prescribed steps — so skills are a discoverable AgentCore entity with a catalog to enumerate and a runtime attachment event to observe, joining Anthropic's `/v1/skills`, Copilot Studio skills and Gemini Enterprise skills in this same week. And it hands Zenity **ready-made detection signals**: custom `TOOL_CALL` evaluators can read the **`invoked_skill`, `skill_content`, `available_skills` and `user_message`** placeholders, which is precisely the join — what the user asked, what skills were on offer, which was chosen, and what it contained — that a detection for skill-driven privilege abuse needs, and it is available without building new instrumentation. AISPM should enumerate the AgentCore skill catalog and treat a skill as an inventory entity with content; AIDR should ingest skill-load tool-call spans as an activity type and consider deriving custom evaluators over the four placeholders to detect a mismatch between user intent and loaded skill

findings.title: AgentCore Coinbase quick create provisions blockchain wallet credentials with no human ever handling the key
findings.description: When creating a Coinbase payment connector, **Quick create** now has AgentCore payments "provision your Coinbase CDP credentials for you" — the operator authorizes access through Coinbase in a browser, and the service **creates the payment credential provider on their behalf**, with no Coinbase API keys generated or pasted by a person. This is a credential-provenance change on a financial capability, and it cuts both ways in a manner Zenity should represent explicitly. It **improves hygiene**: a key that no human ever sees cannot be pasted into a ticket, committed to a repository or shared in chat, which removes the most common failure mode for wallet credentials. It **degrades attribution and reviewability**: the resulting credential provider has no human custodian, its creation is a browser-authorization event rather than a key-management action, and an organization inventorying "who holds wallet credentials" by looking at key custody will find nobody — the answer is the service. Combined with the MPP finding above, the composite picture is an agent that can hold a wallet whose credentials were auto-provisioned and settle metered payments bounded only by a session budget. The asymmetry is also worth recording as a discovery rule: quick create is **Coinbase-only**, while Stripe (Privy) connectors continue to use customer-supplied credentials, so connector type predicts credential provenance. AISPM should inventory payment credential providers with their provenance (quick-created versus supplied), attribute each to the identity that performed the browser authorization rather than to a key holder, and treat a quick-created provider with no named owner as an ownership gap on a financial resource

findings.title: AgentCore Evaluations now runs third-party DeepEval and AutoEval logic, managed or on the customer's own model
findings.description: AgentCore Evaluations added evaluators drawn from the **DeepEval and AutoEval** open-source libraries, usable two ways: select a **managed** third-party evaluator by ID and AWS runs it on a model it operates, exactly like a built-in; or **derive** a custom evaluator from a built-in or third-party evaluator and run its logic on the customer's own model and inference. Both managed and derived third-party evaluators are **discoverable through `ListEvaluators` alongside built-in and custom evaluators**. The coverage point is that the evaluation pipeline — which reads agent inputs, outputs, tool calls and tool results in order to score them — now executes **third-party open-source logic**, and `ListEvaluators` deliberately presents built-in, custom and third-party evaluators in one undifferentiated list. So the provenance of the code judging an agent's behaviour is no longer evident from the inventory surface, and an organization can be running community-maintained evaluation logic over its most sensitive agent traffic without that being visible as a distinct fact. The managed variant additionally means the evaluation runs on **AWS-operated models** rather than the customer's, which is a data-flow the customer did not separately choose. AISPM should enumerate configured evaluators through `ListEvaluators` and **classify each by provenance** — built-in, custom, managed third-party, or derived — flagging third-party evaluators as a supply-chain dependency in the evaluation path, and should record whether a managed evaluator sends agent content to an AWS-operated model

findings.title: Anthropic memory stores now sync into and out of customer-hosted self-hosted sandboxes
findings.description: Claude Managed Agents sessions running in a **self-hosted sandbox** can now attach **memory stores**, and the mechanism is a genuine bidirectional data flow rather than a read: the Python, TypeScript and Go SDK workers **download each attached store into the sandbox at its `mount_path`** and **sync the agent's changes back to the store**. This creates a data path that crosses the boundary between Anthropic-managed state and customer-controlled compute in both directions, and it is the kind of flow that is easy to miss because neither endpoint is new — memory stores existed and self-hosted sandboxes existed; what is new is the sync between them. Three consequences. Memory content now **lands on disk inside customer infrastructure** at a known mount path, so it becomes an on-host artifact subject to the customer's own backup, logging and access controls rather than only Anthropic's. Changes made inside the sandbox — including anything the agent writes, and anything a compromised sandbox writes — **propagate back into the durable memory store** and therefore into future sessions, making the store a persistence mechanism across sessions. And because the sandbox is customer-operated, the integrity of what returns to the store depends on controls Anthropic does not enforce. AIDR should treat memory-store attachment, download and sync-back as distinct activity events and monitor for unexpected write volume; AISPM should discover which agents attach which memory stores to self-hosted sandboxes, record `mount_path` locations as sensitive on-host data locations, and treat a memory store shared across agents or sessions as a cross-session influence channel worth flagging

findings.title: Anthropic added per-tool domain allowlists and blocklists for Managed Agents' web search and web fetch
findings.description: Managed Agents can now restrict which sites the `web_search` and `web_fetch` tools reach, by setting **`allowed_domains` or `blocked_domains`** on the tool's entry in the `agent_toolset_20260401` **`configs`** array; `web_fetch` additionally accepts **`max_content_tokens`** and `web_search` accepts `user_location`. Each `configs` entry is identified by its `name` and typed by an optional `type`, and entries passing only `name`, `enabled` and `permission_policy` keep working — so this is an additive extension of a configuration surface Zenity should already be reading. This is a **control** rather than a new capability, which is exactly why it belongs in posture coverage: the presence, absence and content of these lists is now a measurable property of every Managed Agent with web access. An agent with `web_fetch` and no `allowed_domains` can retrieve arbitrary internet content into its context, which is the primary indirect-injection path for this class of agent; an agent with a tight allowlist is materially safer, and that difference is discoverable. `max_content_tokens` is a secondary signal — it bounds how much untrusted retrieved content can enter the context per fetch. The typed-`configs` change also means Zenity's parsing of this array should not assume the old three-key shape. AISPM should read the `configs` array per agent, record whether each web tool is domain-restricted and by which list, flag web-enabled agents with no restriction as an elevated injection-exposure class, and treat a change that widens or removes an allowlist as a posture regression worth alerting on

findings.title: Anthropic's Claude Enterprise user-management Admin API went GA — members, invites, groups and custom roles
findings.description: The **Admin API** user-management endpoints for **Claude Enterprise (claude.ai) organizations** — members, invites, **groups** and **custom roles** — are now generally available, with the `ce-user-management-2026-07-13` beta header no longer required. This is the identity and authorization surface for the enterprise Claude tenant, and its GA matters to Zenity for a straightforward reason: it is now a stable, non-beta API path to enumerate **who is in the organization, what groups they belong to, and what custom roles grant them** — the join Zenity needs to attribute observed agent activity to a governed identity and to evaluate whether that identity's privileges are appropriate. **Custom roles** are the part deserving specific attention: a custom role is a customer-defined permission set, so the meaning of a role is not fixed across tenants and cannot be inferred from its name — Zenity must read the role's actual permissions rather than pattern-matching a label, and an over-broad custom role is a posture finding that only appears if the permissions are resolved. Groups matter as the mechanism through which access is granted at scale, so a group's membership is the real blast radius of any grant made to it. Read alongside the Compliance API local-session work from 2026-08-14, this completes a usable pair: the Compliance API supplies agent activity keyed on `user.id`, and the Admin API resolves that ID to a member, their groups and their effective roles. AISPM should enumerate members, invites, groups and custom roles, resolve each custom role to its concrete permissions, flag over-privileged roles and stale invites, and join identities to Compliance API session activity

findings.title: Copilot Studio can export environment-level agent telemetry to Azure Application Insights
findings.description: Copilot Studio added a preview capability to export **environment-level agent telemetry** to **Azure Application Insights**, configured through the **Power Platform admin center**. This is an ingestion opportunity and a posture attribute in one. As ingestion: it is a first-party, admin-configured, environment-wide path for Copilot Studio agent telemetry to reach a destination Zenity can already read, rather than requiring per-agent instrumentation or scraping the Copilot Studio UI — and because it is scoped to the environment, enabling it once covers every agent in that environment, including agents created later. As posture: whether an environment has telemetry export configured determines whether agent behaviour there is observable at all, so an environment **without** it is a monitoring blind spot that Zenity should report as a gap in its own right, particularly for environments hosting autonomous or externally-facing agents. Two practical notes. Because configuration happens in the Power Platform admin center rather than per agent, the setting lives with the platform administrator and is discoverable at tenant scope. And the Foundry precedent from 2026-08-14 should be applied here rather than rediscovered: agent telemetry carrying prompts, tool definitions, tool arguments and tool results is sensitive content, and Foundry is relocating exactly those attributes into a protected `AppGenAIContent` table by September 30, 2026 — so Zenity should establish up front which Application Insights tables Copilot Studio's export writes to, and who can read them. AIDR should add Copilot Studio's Application Insights export as an ingestion source; AISPM should discover which environments have it enabled and flag those that do not

findings.title: Microsoft opened an MCP server certification program for Copilot Studio
findings.description: Publishers can now **submit an MCP server for Microsoft certification**, to "give customers and administrators confidence that it meets Microsoft's expectations for reliability, security, compliance, and responsible operation" (preview). This creates a **new trust attribute** on an entity type Zenity already inventories, and it arrives in the same release that lets Copilot Studio agents attach MCP servers as tools — so certification status becomes a usable posture signal precisely when MCP attachment becomes easy. The parallel to draw is Foundry's connector publisher tiers, reported 2026-08-14, where Microsoft's own documentation distinguishes internal, external, verified third-party and independent publishers "at a lower certification bar", and where the portal gated only validated connectors while the REST/SDK path had no gating at all. The same question applies here and should be answered rather than assumed: whether an uncertified MCP server can still be attached, and through which paths. Certification is also a **point-in-time attestation about a continuously-changing remote service** — an MCP server's tool list, prompts and backing implementation can change after certification without re-review — so the attribute should be recorded with its date and treated as weaker evidence than a live inspection of the server's advertised tools. AISPM should record certification status and date per attached MCP server as an inventory attribute, flag uncertified servers attached to agents holding sensitive connections, and detect changes in a certified server's advertised tool list as a signal that the attestation no longer describes what is deployed

findings.title: AgentCore Memory is now wired into Bedrock knowledge-base agentic retrieval via `memoryConfiguration`
findings.description: Agentic retrieval on fully managed Amazon Bedrock knowledge bases now integrates with **AgentCore Memory** through a **`memoryConfiguration`** field on the **`AgenticRetrieveStream`** API. Three modes are documented: restore an earlier session from **short-term memory**, let the agent **retrieve memory records from long-term memory**, or both. This is a cross-service data flow between two surfaces Zenity tracks separately, and the direction is the part that matters — **memory content flows into the retrieval path**, so what an agent retrieves from a knowledge base is now conditioned on persisted memory from prior sessions. Two consequences follow. **Retrieval results become session-history-dependent**, meaning the same query against the same knowledge base can return different content depending on what memory was attached, which breaks the assumption that a knowledge base's effective exposure can be evaluated from its own permissions alone. And **memory becomes a durable influence channel on retrieval**: a record written to long-term memory in one session shapes retrieval in later ones, so memory poisoning has a retrieval-side effect and not merely a conversational one. The session-restore mode additionally means conversation state from an earlier session is re-hydrated into a new one, which is a data-lineage question for any organization that believes sessions are isolated. AIDR should treat `AgenticRetrieveStream` calls carrying `memoryConfiguration` as a joined memory-plus-retrieval activity and record both the memory resource and the knowledge base; AISPM should map which AgentCore Memory resources are attached to which knowledge bases, and flag long-term memory feeding retrieval over sensitive knowledge bases

findings.title: Cursor Cloud Agents now self-subscribe to PRs and Slack threads, run scheduled tasks, and spawn subagents on isolated machines
findings.description: Cursor's August 19 Cloud Agents release adds autonomy primitives that change what a Cursor agent is, for a watching-tier platform. **Subscriptions** let agents monitor **PRs, Slack threads and scheduled tasks**, and agents **automatically subscribe to PRs they create and drive them to completion** — so an agent's work is no longer bounded by a human-initiated session; it acquires a standing trigger on artifacts it produced itself. **`/goal`** assigns long-lived objectives that agents "work toward independently". **Subagents now run on isolated machines**, each in its own virtual environment with a clean project copy, which multiplies the compute identities acting on a repository from one per task to many. **Custom Modes** are described as "always on" skills. Non-interruptive steering queues human guidance for the next tool call instead of halting execution — a small but real reduction in the human's ability to stop work in progress. The coverage consequences are: agent activity becomes **continuous and event-triggered rather than session-bounded**, so an inventory of "agents" is less meaningful than an inventory of **active subscriptions and goals**; **Slack thread monitoring** puts an agent on a channel where untrusted text arrives, which is an injection path into an agent holding repository access; and subagents on isolated machines mean the principal acting on code is frequently not the one a human authorized. AISPM should discover Cursor Cloud Agent subscriptions, goals and scheduled tasks as standing-authorization entities, resolve which repositories and Slack workspaces each reaches, and flag self-created PR subscriptions as autonomous action; AIRT should test Slack-thread-sourced injection into subscribed agents

findings.title: Codex CLI added Amazon Bedrock Runtime as a built-in provider, compounding a documented Anthropic capture blind spot
findings.description: Codex CLI 0.148.0 added **Amazon Bedrock Runtime as a built-in provider**, so a developer can point OpenAI's coding agent at Bedrock-hosted models with no third-party shim. On its own this is a routing convenience; in combination with two facts already established in this monitor it is a coverage problem worth naming. First, Anthropic's Compliance API — the surface reported on 2026-08-14 as the richest available source of local Claude Code and Cowork session transcripts — **explicitly does not capture Claude Code routed through Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud or Microsoft Foundry**. Second, as of this scan `bedrock-runtime` **serves the Anthropic Messages API directly** on its `/anthropic` route. So a developer using Codex CLI against Bedrock Runtime with a Claude model produces agent activity that is invisible to Anthropic's compliance surface, arrives at AWS in Anthropic's wire format on an endpoint whose parser selection Zenity is only now correcting, and originates from OpenAI's client rather than Anthropic's. Each vendor's own telemetry sees at most a fragment. The general lesson is that **built-in cross-provider routing in local agent clients breaks per-vendor observability**, and the mitigation is endpoint-side rather than client-side: coverage has to come from the AWS account's own logging, not from either model vendor. Also in the same release: **asynchronous MCP tool invocation in hooks**, which lets an MCP tool call run without blocking hook execution. ENDPOINT should detect Codex CLI provider configuration on developer machines and identify Bedrock-routed configurations as a case where vendor-side compliance capture does not apply; AIDR should ensure Bedrock-side logging covers traffic originating from Codex CLI

findings.title: OpenAI Computer History is now available in the EEA, Switzerland and the UK
findings.description: **Computer History** — the macOS feature reported on 2026-08-14 that turns interaction events across every app and website into memories via an ephemeral Codex session, requiring macOS accessibility access and writing plain-text memory files to local disk — is now available to **Pro, Business and Enterprise users in the EEA, Switzerland and the UK**, the three jurisdictions explicitly excluded at launch eight days ago. The capability itself is unchanged, so this is an extension rather than a new surface, but the extension is the part that matters for coverage: those exclusions were the reason European deployments could be treated as out of scope, and that reason is gone. Every control this monitor recorded for it now needs to be evaluated against European data-protection expectations — a desktop-wide keystroke-and-interaction recorder whose events are **processed on OpenAI servers** before local memory files are written is a materially different proposition under GDPR than under US practice, and the workspace-level admin grant required for Business and Enterprise is the control that determines whether it can be enabled at all in those tenants. ENDPOINT should extend Computer History detection to European endpoints rather than treating the feature as US-only, and should surface the per-app and per-website contribution settings, since those determine what an enabled instance actually captures; AISPM should track the workspace admin grant as a tenant control and flag European workspaces where it has been granted, so that decision is visible to whoever owns the data-protection position rather than resting with individual users

findings.title: Anthropic's computer use tool went GA with batch actions and per-member configuration
findings.description: The **computer use tool** is now generally available on the Claude API as **`computer_toolset_20260801`**, dropping the beta header. Three changes accompany GA: **batch actions**, letting several actions run in one turn; **`zoom` enabled by default**; and **per-member configuration through `configs`**. Earlier beta versions remain available, and Anthropic notes that upgrading an existing integration changes the request shape and tool handling. Both this and the new browser toolset are available on Claude Fable 5, Claude Mythos 5, Claude Opus 5, Claude Sonnet 5 and Claude Opus 4.8. The reportable substance is GA plus the two structural changes. Removing the beta header removes the last friction on granting a model full desktop control, so prevalence should be expected to rise. **Batch actions** matter for detection: several actions now execute per turn without an intervening model round-trip, which compresses the window in which an interposed control could evaluate an action before the next one runs — a monitor that assumes one action per turn will under-count and will observe consequences later than it expects. **Per-member `configs`** is the useful half: individual members of the toolset can be configured separately, which means Zenity can read which capabilities are actually enabled on a given deployment rather than treating "computer use" as a single boolean. AISPM should discover deployments using `computer_toolset_20260801`, enumerate the enabled members and their per-member configuration as privileged capability, and flag deployments still on beta versions since their request shape and handling differ; AIDR should parse batched actions as multiple discrete activity events within one turn

findings.title: Gemini Enterprise Agent Registry governs `Endpoints` as a record type, with IAM governance policies in private preview
findings.description: The Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform's **Agent Registry** — the central inventory for the platform — catalogs four entity types, and the one this monitor has not covered is **`Endpoints`**: "target destinations to centrally govern the external APIs and services that your agents can connect to", alongside **MCP servers**, **tools** and **agents**. An **auth manager and bindings** authenticate agents to discovered tools, and **new IAM governance policies entered private preview** in August. Endpoints are worth specific attention because they are the registry's representation of **egress** — the set of external services an agent is permitted to reach — which makes the registry not just an inventory of what exists but a policy object describing where agent traffic may go. That is the same question Zenity answers from the agent side, so for customers on this platform there are two authoritative-looking answers to "what can this agent reach", and divergence between them is a finding in either direction. The **auth manager and bindings** are the second half: a binding is where an agent's identity is joined to a discovered tool's credential, so bindings are the concrete grant records that determine effective reach, and enumerating them is how you get from "this tool is discoverable" to "this agent can actually call it". The IAM governance policies being **private preview** means they are not yet generally observable, and should be tracked rather than assumed absent. AISPM should enumerate Agent Registry records by `recordType` including Endpoints, resolve auth-manager bindings to determine each agent's effective tool and endpoint reach, reconcile registry-declared egress against observed traffic, and watch for the IAM governance policies reaching public preview

findings.title: Salesforce Winter '27 adds dedicated Agentforce marketing agents and renames Agentforce Lead Nurturing to Agentforce Engagement
findings.description: Winter '27 release notes published on their expected date of **August 19**, and introduce **two Agentforce agents dedicated to marketing**, the first being a **Marketing Goals Agent** that translates business objectives into actionable marketing strategies. **Agentforce Lead Nurturing is renamed Agentforce Engagement**, a new version of **Agentforce Builder** ships, and an AI **call-coaching agent** that automatically evaluates recorded calls and gives reps feedback is available with Agentforce for Sales. For Zenity the new prebuilt agents are new inventory entities with their own default action sets and data reach — a marketing-strategy agent touches campaign and prospect data, and a call-coaching agent reads **recorded customer calls**, which is among the more sensitive data classes an agent can be given standing access to. The **rename is a concrete detection hazard** of the kind this monitor has flagged before with ServiceNow's Vertex connector: any Zenity logic matching "Agentforce Lead Nurturing" by display name will silently stop matching, and the underlying agent is the same object. **Two caveats bound this finding.** It rests on **WebSearch corroboration only** — every Salesforce source failed this scan (`salesforce.com/releases/` 403, the Agentforce developer guide 503 for a second consecutive scan, `help.salesforce.com` returned a render error) — so the technical specifics must be verified next scan before being acted on. And **"MCP interoperability for Agentforce", which appears in Salesforce's feature-availability listing, carries a release date of the week of May 18, 2026** and is therefore not a Winter '27 addition; it is excluded here deliberately. AISPM should add the new prebuilt agents to its Agentforce inventory once verified, match agents on stable identifiers rather than display names, and treat the call-coaching agent's access to call recordings as a sensitive data flow

platforms.name: Claude Enterprise (Anthropic) — live changelog, two new entries
details: **Compliance API returns local session transcripts (Aug 11, beta, Claude Enterprise only).** Three endpoints — `GET /v1/compliance/apps/sessions/local` (list, `clls_` IDs), `GET /v1/compliance/apps/sessions/local/{session_id}` (metadata), `GET /v1/compliance/apps/sessions/local/{session_id}/messages` (transcript). Uses the **existing Compliance Access Key and `read:compliance_user_data` scope — no new key, scope, setting or client update**. Admin API keys are rejected with 403. `product_surface` is `cowork` (Claude Desktop) or `claude_code` (terminal, Desktop, or IDE extension). Transcripts contain user prompts, assistant text, `tool_use` and `tool_result` blocks, with **MCP tool calls and most server tool calls normalized into those same shapes**; `CLAUDE.md` appears as ordinary user content and skill content appears when the client sends it. Excluded: thinking blocks, the system prompt (a synthetic marker stands in), **tool definitions and MCP server configuration**, and all binary blocks. Retention 6 years or the org's custom conversation retention period. Read-only — no deletion through the API. Source: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/compliance-sessions#retrieve-local-sessions

**`anthropic-workspace-id` response header (Aug 11).** Every Claude API response now carries the `wrkspc_`-prefixed ID of the workspace that the request's API key or access token resolved to, including the organization's Default Workspace. Source: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/workspaces
*(Not reported: Aug 10 Claude Sonnet 5 pricing decision — pricing.)*

platforms.name: Microsoft Foundry — roll-up unfroze; five new agent-platform surfaces
details: **Enable incoming A2A on a Foundry agent (preview)** — ms.date 2026-08-12, updated 2026-08-13, the freshest item in this scan. Exposes an agent **as** an A2A server; this monitor had previously only covered the outgoing direction. Enabled by a single PATCH setting `agent_card` plus `agent_endpoint.protocol_configuration.a2a`; **not available in the Foundry portal**, REST/SDK only. Serves **both A2A v1.0 and v0.3 on the same base path**, with version chosen by agent-card discovery, the `A2A-Version` header, or `?a2a-version=` — and **v0.3 is served by default when unspecified**. Cards are published at `…/protocols/a2a/agentCard/v1.0` and `…/agentCard/v0.3`, carrying description, version and a **`skills[]`** array. All A2A URLs require Entra ID auth (**anonymous agent-card access is not supported**) and the caller needs **Foundry Agent Consumer** or higher. Callers authenticate either **on-behalf-of the end user** or with a **service identity**. v1.0 is JSONRPC-only; text modality only; no streaming. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/how-to/enable-agent-to-agent-endpoint

**Managed MCP servers powered by connector namespaces (preview)** — ms.date 2026-07-28. The Foundry Tools Catalog carries **over 1,000 connectors**; adding one makes Foundry provision a **managed MCP server**.
