findings.title: Anthropic Compliance API now exposes transcripts of Cowork and Claude Code sessions running on employee laptops
findings.description: Three new endpoints — `GET /v1/compliance/apps/sessions/local`, `.../local/{session_id}`, and `.../local/{session_id}/messages` — return the full conversation of agent sessions that execute **on users' own machines**, for Claude Enterprise organizations. Transcripts carry user prompts, assistant text, and **`tool_use` and `tool_result` blocks, with MCP tool calls and most server tool calls normalized into those same shapes**, so an agent's actual tool invocations and their returned data are readable. `product_surface` distinguishes `cowork` from `claude_code`, `CLAUDE.md` project instructions appear as ordinary user content, and skill content appears when the client sends it. This is the richest AIDR ingestion surface Anthropic has published and it requires **no new credential** — it reuses the same Compliance Access Key and `read:compliance_user_data` scope Zenity may already hold, and no client-side deployment. Two things demand equal attention. First, **the documented blind spots are a coverage map in themselves**: Claude Code authenticated with a Console API key or routed through **Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud or Microsoft Foundry** is not captured, nor is Claude Code on the web, nor anything in organizations with **HIPAA readiness** or under **ZDR**, and under **CMEK** sessions list but their content is withheld — so an enterprise can believe it has full local-agent visibility while its Bedrock-routed developers are entirely invisible. Second, **what is deliberately omitted from every transcript matters for detection**: thinking blocks, the system prompt, and — most significantly — **tool definitions and MCP server configuration**, meaning a transcript shows that a tool was called but never what that tool was permitted to do or which MCP server backed it. AIDR should ingest local sessions as a first-class agent-activity stream keyed on `product_surface`, join `user.id` to identity, and treat the excluded populations as explicit gaps to close by other means; AISPM should discover whether HIPAA/ZDR/CMEK settings are suppressing capture, since each silently disables it

findings.title: Microsoft Foundry agents can now be published as callable A2A servers with discoverable agent cards
findings.description: Foundry has added **incoming A2A** — the ability to expose an agent **as** an Agent2Agent endpoint that other agents discover and call — updated two days before this scan and the freshest change in it. Every prompt agent supports it by default, and enabling it takes a single PATCH that sets `agent_card` and adds `a2a` to `protocol_configuration`; it is **not exposed in the Foundry portal at all**, so it can only be turned on via REST or SDK and will be invisible to anyone auditing through the UI. The agent then publishes cards at `…/protocols/a2a/agentCard/v1.0` and `…/agentCard/v0.3` advertising its description and a **`skills[]` capability list** to any authorized caller. The finding Zenity most needs is the **version-negotiation default**: Foundry serves **both v1.0 and v0.3 on the same base path**, and **when a caller specifies no version, it serves v0.3** — so the protocol actually spoken on an endpoint is chosen by the *caller*, not by the endpoint's configuration, and an inventory that records "A2A v1.0" from the configuration will be wrong for any client that doesn't negotiate. The authorization model is the second half: all A2A URLs require Entra ID (**anonymous agent-card access is explicitly unsupported**, which is a genuine control worth verifying rather than assuming), callers need only **Foundry Agent Consumer** on the hosting project, and they may authenticate either **on-behalf-of an end user** or **with a service identity** — the latter meaning an agent-to-agent call chain with no human in it and no user context to scope against. AISPM should discover which agents have `a2a` in their `protocol_configuration`, inventory each published `agent_card` and its `skills[]` as the agent's advertised attack surface, enumerate every principal holding Foundry Agent Consumer as a potential caller, and flag agents reachable by service identity. AIRT should treat a published agent card as a discovery primitive and test whether inbound A2A content is handled as trusted instruction

findings.title: Microsoft Foundry connector namespaces turn 1,000+ SaaS connectors into auto-provisioned managed MCP servers hosted on logic.azure.com
findings.description: Adding any connector from the Foundry Tools Catalog now causes Foundry to provision a **managed MCP server** on the customer's behalf. Every Foundry account has a **Connector Namespace** — a managed service hosting connector runtimes and MCP servers — with **each project mapped to its own environment** inside it, and the namespace owns server hosting, tool definitions, authentication, credential management and lifecycle. Three properties make this a first-order inventory problem. First, **scale and provenance**: over 1,000 connectors span four publisher tiers with explicitly different data-handling — Microsoft internal (SharePoint, Teams, Dynamics 365), Microsoft external (GitHub), verified third-party (Docusign, Databricks, Box), and **independent publishers at what Microsoft calls a "lower certification bar"** — so the publisher tier of each attached connector is a posture signal, and Microsoft's own page warns that auth keys and prompt content may be passed to third-party tools and that "MCP implementations are vulnerable to attacks, cascading failures, and loss of human oversight." Second, **the endpoint is not where you would look for it**: the connection's `target` is rewritten from a literal `https://placeholder` to a **`logic.azure.com/api/connectorGateways/<envId>/mcpServerConfigs/<name>/mcp`** URL, so the real MCP endpoint lives on Logic Apps infrastructure, not on the Foundry project endpoint, and the connection is identifiable by `metadata.type = gateway_connector` with `category: RemoteTool`. Third, **the portal's safety rail does not exist in code**: only *validated* connectors surface the managed-MCP experience in the portal, but the docs state plainly that via REST, SDK or `azd` **"there's no gating — you can use any connector in the catalog."** Add that each end user must complete a **per-user OAuth consent**, so the effective reach of a tool is the union of every consenting user's permissions in the target SaaS. AISPM should enumerate project connections of type `gateway_connector`, resolve each to its connector, publisher tier and **registered operation list** (`mcpserverConfigProperties`), record the logic.azure.com gateway target as an inventory endpoint, flag connectors added through the code-first path that would not have passed portal validation, and treat write-capable operations as privileged

findings.title: OpenAI Computer History records everything a user does on macOS and feeds it to an ephemeral Codex agent
findings.description: ChatGPT's macOS desktop app has shipped an opt-in feature that converts **activity across all apps and websites** into memories and a timeline usable by ChatGPT and Codex. It records interaction events exposed through **macOS accessibility APIs** — clicks, typing, keyboard shortcuts, and app switching — which means keystrokes and UI interactions inside applications that have nothing to do with ChatGPT, including other security tools, terminals, password managers and internal business systems. The architecture is the finding: events are buffered on the Mac for up to 48 hours, and Computer History then **periodically starts an ephemeral Codex session with access to the raw interaction-event stream** to summarize it into memories; those temporary event files are **processed on OpenAI's servers** before the resulting **plain-text memory files are written back to local disk**, where they persist until deleted. So a general-purpose agent session is granted a feed of the user's entire desktop activity, and a durable plain-text derivative of it sits on the endpoint. It replaces the Chronicle preview and is a genuine rebuild — Chronicle captured screenshots, this does not, and it also excludes screen recordings, microphone and system audio — but the accessibility-event stream is arguably more sensitive than screenshots because it captures typed content directly. Governance hooks exist and should be inventoried: it is **off by default**, Pro users may self-enable, and **Business and Enterprise workspaces require an administrator to grant access before any member can turn it on**; users choose which apps and websites contribute and can pause collection from the menu bar; it is unavailable in the EEA, Switzerland and the UK. ENDPOINT should detect the ChatGPT macOS app's Computer History state per device, inventory the local memory files as a sensitive on-disk artifact, and alert when it is enabled on endpoints with access to regulated systems; AISPM should track the workspace-level admin grant as a tenant control; AIRT should consider whether content typed in one application can shape agent behaviour in another through the resulting memories

findings.title: OpenAI Daybreak Red grants access to GPT-5.6-Cyber, a model that answers 95% of exploit-development prompts
findings.description: OpenAI has added two tiers to its Daybreak "Trusted Access for Cyber" program. **Daybreak Blue** covers approved defensive workflows — secure code review, vulnerability triage, detection engineering, incident response, malware analysis, patch validation — on GPT-5.6 Sol with system-level safeguards. **Daybreak Red** goes further, covering advanced defensive **and offensive** cyber tasks with access to the purpose-trained **GPT-5.5-Cyber and GPT-5.6-Cyber** models for vulnerability research, exploit validation and security testing. The number that matters for Zenity is OpenAI's own published evaluation: **GPT-5.6-Cyber handled 95% of advanced cybersecurity prompts** spanning exploit-chain development, authentication bypass and privilege escalation, **while GPT-5.6 Sol with default protections answered 1.5%**. That is an explicit, vendor-documented ~63x differential in offensive capability gated only by program membership, and it changes the threat model in both directions. Defensively, a tenant where some identity holds Daybreak Red access has a materially different risk profile from one that does not, and that entitlement is a posture attribute Zenity should be able to discover and attest — including which users or service accounts hold it and whether their use is logged. Offensively, this is directly relevant to AIRT's own mandate: the capability differential defines a realistic upper bound for what an attacker with a compromised Red-tier credential could do against a customer's agents and infrastructure, and it makes the Daybreak entitlement itself a high-value credential worth protecting like any other. AIRT should incorporate the Blue/Red capability distinction into red-team scenario design and use the published differential to calibrate assumed adversary capability; AISPM should inventory Daybreak tier membership as a privileged entitlement on the OpenAI organization alongside admin roles

findings.title: Amazon Bedrock has a second inference endpoint — `bedrock-mantle` — serving OpenAI and Anthropic APIs with stateful conversations, and AWS now recommends it over `bedrock-runtime`
findings.description: `bedrock-mantle.<region>.api.aws`, powered by "Project Mantle", is a distributed inference engine running in parallel to `bedrock-runtime` and serving three API shapes Zenity's Bedrock coverage was not built for: the **OpenAI Responses API**, the **OpenAI Chat Completions API**, and the **Anthropic Messages API**. It adds **built-in tool use and stateful conversation management**, and AWS's stated migration pitch is that an existing OpenAI SDK codebase moves onto Bedrock by changing only the base URL and API key. AWS **recommends bedrock-mantle for new applications**, which means new Bedrock workloads will default onto it. This is a coverage gap rather than a fresh launch — it surfaced only because an August 11 cost-allocation note named it, but PrivateLink support for these endpoints landed in February 2026 and dedicated CloudWatch metrics and a redesigned console in June 2026, so the surface has been building for roughly six months while every scan looked at `bedrock-runtime` and the Agents APIs. Three consequences follow. Detection keyed on `bedrock-runtime` API shapes will **silently miss all mantle traffic**, and because the request/response formats are OpenAI's and Anthropic's rather than AWS's, parsing differs too. **Stateful conversation management** means conversation state now lives server-side in Bedrock, a data store that did not previously exist in this service and that Zenity does not inventory. And **built-in tool use** means tool invocation happens inside the endpoint, so the tool-call surface is not visible in the customer's own orchestration code. AISPM should add the mantle endpoint to Bedrock discovery, inventory IAM principals and PrivateLink endpoints reaching it, and reconcile mantle usage against known agent inventory; AIDR should add parsers for the OpenAI Responses, Chat Completions and Anthropic Messages shapes on this endpoint and treat its stateful conversations as a retained data location

findings.title: Gemini Enterprise Skills are shareable packages that can carry scripts and files, not just instructions
findings.description: Gemini Enterprise now lets users **create, upload and share skills**. The critical detail is the packaging model: each skill is a **package containing a `SKILL.md` prompt file**, and the package **can also include scripts, files, or background context** the assistant uses to complete the task. That makes a skill a distributable artifact that carries executable and data content between users, not merely a saved prompt — and it is a new inventory entity type with an owner, a body, attachments and a sharing graph. The sharing model is the governance surface: an administrator must enable the skills feature, and must **separately enable skill sharing**, which can be configured either to **require administrator review** or to **allow immediate sharing** — so whether a user-authored package containing scripts can propagate across the organization unreviewed is a single tenant toggle. Sharing itself is per-user by email address, producing exactly the kind of informal distribution graph that outruns governance. A programmatic **Skill Registry** exists on the Agent Platform side, giving Zenity an API path to enumerate them. AISPM should discover skills as an entity type with owner, contents and share list, record whether the tenant requires administrator review before sharing (and flag tenants that do not), inspect skill packages for scripts and embedded credentials, and treat a widely-shared skill as a high-blast-radius object. AIRT should treat skill content as an injection vector, since a shared skill's `SKILL.md` becomes instruction text in every recipient's agent context

findings.title: Gemini Enterprise GitHub connector reaches GA with write access to source control — merge pull requests, push files, create branches
findings.description: The GitHub connector is now generally available with **data federation**, and its action set is the finding: **create branch, create or update file, push file, update pull request, merge pull request, fork repository, update issues, add comment to an issue, add comment to a pending review**. An agent with this connector attached can therefore **modify source code and merge changes into repositories** — one of the highest-consequence write paths an enterprise agent can hold, since merged code reaches CI/CD and production. This is materially different from the read-only search connectors that make up most of the catalog and should not be inventoried in the same class. The federation mechanism adds a second consideration: rather than indexing content into a data store, Gemini Enterprise **sends the search query directly to the GitHub API at query time** and blends the results, which means access is evaluated live against the connecting credential and there is no indexed copy to inspect — so the connector's effective read scope is exactly whatever its GitHub credential can see, at the moment of query, and cannot be determined from a data-store inventory. AISPM should discover GitHub connector instances, resolve the authenticating GitHub identity and its repository scopes, enumerate which of the write actions are enabled on each agent, and flag any agent holding `merge pull request` or `push file` as a code-integrity risk requiring branch-protection compensating controls. AIRT should test whether prompt injection reaching such an agent can drive a merge or a file push

findings.title: Microsoft Foundry is relocating prompts, tool definitions, tool arguments and tool results into a separate protected trace table by September 30, 2026
findings.description: Foundry now classifies seven OpenTelemetry gen-AI attributes as sensitive content — `gen_ai.input.messages`, `gen_ai.output.messages`, `gen_ai.system_instructions`, **`gen_ai.tool.definitions`**, **`gen_ai.tool.call.arguments`**, **`gen_ai.tool.call.result`**, and `gen_ai.evaluation.explanation` — and routes them to a dedicated Log Analytics table, **`AppGenAIContent`**, which can be marked **Protected** so that only holders of the **Privileged Monitoring Data Reader** role can read it. This is both an operational deadline and a posture control. Operationally: **starting September 30, 2026, these attribute values stop being written to `AppDependencies`, `AppTraces` and `AppEvents` for newly ingested data** — the keys remain but the values are replaced with a short pointer to `AppGenAIContent`. **Any Zenity query, detection or ingestion path reading Foundry agent prompts, tool calls or tool results from those three tables will silently return pointers instead of content after that date**, which is a hard-dated breakage rather than a gradual drift, and the opt-out flag that defers it is itself discontinued on September 30, 2027. As posture: whether a customer has set `AppGenAIContent` to Protected, and who holds Privileged Monitoring Data Reader on it, determines who in the organization can read every prompt, system instruction and tool result their agents have produced — an unprotected table means standard Log Analytics readers can read all of it, and an over-broad grant of the privileged role is a serious exposure. AIDR should migrate Foundry trace ingestion to `AppGenAIContent` ahead of the deadline and ensure its identity holds the privileged role where the table is protected; AISPM should discover the table's protection level per workspace, inventory Privileged Monitoring Data Reader assignments as privileged access to agent conversation content, and flag workspaces where agent traces remain readable by standard roles

findings.title: ChatGPT desktop imports agent configuration — settings, skills, plugins and projects — from Claude Code, Claude Cowork and Cursor, with continuous sync
findings.description: The ChatGPT desktop app can now import **instructions, settings, skills, plugins, projects and recent work** from **Claude Code, Claude Cowork and Cursor**, and can be set to keep imported work **automatically in sync with the original agent**; Codex CLI offers the same via `/import` for Claude Code and Cursor. This matters to ENDPOINT coverage because it breaks the assumption that each local agent's configuration is independently governed. A skill, plugin or instruction set that was reviewed and approved in one tool now propagates into another vendor's agent — and with automatic updates on, it keeps propagating, so a change made in Cursor can land in ChatGPT without any further user action. Practically: a policy that governs Claude Code's plugins does not govern the copies now running under ChatGPT, and configuration drift between the two is invisible unless both are inventoried and compared. It also creates a lateral path for a malicious or compromised skill to spread across the endpoint's agent estate from a single point of entry. ENDPOINT should inventory local agent configurations per tool rather than per machine, detect whether import and automatic updates are enabled in the ChatGPT desktop app, and treat a skill or plugin present in two agents as one object with two enforcement points — reconciling them so an approval in one tool is not silently inherited by another

findings.title: Microsoft Foundry Canvas builds and deploys production Foundry agents from inside the GitHub Copilot App
findings.description: Foundry Canvas is a **GitHub Copilot App extension** that opens a side panel to design, configure, test and deploy Foundry **hosted agents** without leaving the editor. It signs the developer in to Azure, enumerates their subscriptions and Foundry projects, and browses the project's deployed models, **toolboxes, tools, skills and guardrails**, letting them be attached to a new agent; each choice becomes a prompt for Copilot, which writes the agent code. **Inspect Locally** runs the agent in an embedded **Agent Inspector**, and **Deploy to Foundry** publishes it — both by executing underlying `azd` commands. The coverage point is that a developer's IDE is now a **provisioning path into the customer's cloud agent estate**: agents can be created, wired to real tools and guardrails, and deployed to Foundry from a local editor extension, so agent creation events will originate from developer workstations rather than the portal or a CI pipeline, and the guardrail selection for a production agent is made in an editor side panel. The extension is installed from the Copilot App's plugin marketplace by searching `microsoft-foundry`, which is itself a supply-chain consideration for an extension holding Azure credentials. ENDPOINT should detect Foundry Canvas installation on developer endpoints and treat it as an agent-provisioning tool; AISPM should correlate Foundry agent-creation events back to the identity and workstation that ran `azd`, and flag agents deployed this way whose guardrail configuration diverges from policy

findings.title: Gemini Enterprise adds 12 data-source connectors and turns four read-only connectors into write-capable ones
findings.description: Twelve new data stores entered public preview — **Cisco Workspaces, Fibery, Gong, Guru, Hex, LegalZoom, Mercury, Miro, Ramp, Solve Intelligence, Vanta and Webex Meetings** — each extending the agent's reach into a new third-party system with natural-language search and read operations. Several carry unusually sensitive content for an agent to reach: **Gong** holds recorded sales conversations, **Mercury** and **Ramp** are financial systems, **LegalZoom** and **Solve Intelligence** hold legal and IP material, and **Vanta** holds the organization's own compliance and security posture data — an agent that can read Vanta can read the customer's control evidence and gaps. Separately, four existing connectors gained **write** actions: Airtable record updates, Hex threads, Miro document creation and Smartsheet row additions — meaning connectors previously inventoried as read-only now mutate third-party state, and any classification Zenity recorded for them is stale. AISPM should add the twelve connectors to its Gemini Enterprise inventory with data-sensitivity classification, re-evaluate the four changed connectors' read/write classification rather than trusting cached values, resolve the authenticating identity and scope for each connector instance, and flag agents holding write actions into financial or compliance systems

findings.title: ServiceNow AI Control Tower adds an agent map spanning models, MCP servers and cross-cloud providers, plus AI asset deduplication
findings.description: The Australia Patch 4 release of AI Control Tower adds an **agent map visualization** displaying **models, MCP servers, providers and workflows** across the enterprise, and a **deduplication** capability that identifies redundant AI assets for consolidation. Both are directly comparable to AISPM's own output, and both were absent from the prior scan's read of this page. The agent map matters because it explicitly includes **MCP servers** as first-class mapped entities alongside models and workflows — ServiceNow is building the same topology graph Zenity produces, sourced from its Service Graph connectors rather than from direct platform integration, which means for customers running both there will be two topology graphs of the same estate with different fidelity and different blind spots. Deduplication is the more actionable of the two: it presumes ServiceNow can tell when two discovered assets are the same underlying agent or model, which is precisely the reconciliation problem Zenity faces when correlating its own inventory against a customer's CMDB. AISPM should treat the ServiceNow agent map as a comparison inventory to reconcile against — divergence in either direction is a reportable finding — and should ingest deduplication decisions rather than recomputing them, so Zenity and ServiceNow do not disagree about how many agents a customer has

findings.title: ServiceNow AI Service Graph Connectors gain versioned per-vendor capabilities, including a Databricks connector that imports agents and an Anthropic connector that tracks per-user cost
findings.description: The connector set behind AI Control Tower now has stated versions and differentiated capabilities: **Anthropic v2.0.7** discovers models and tracks **per-user costs**, **GCP Vertex AI v1.2.4** has been renamed **"AI Connector for Google"**, **Microsoft** uses a unified Azure ML configuration with **certificate-based authentication**, **Amazon** consolidates to a single credential page with **automatic key rotation**, and **Databricks discovers *and imports* AI agents**. Two details raise this above routine connector churn. The Databricks connector **imports** agents rather than merely discovering them, meaning ServiceNow becomes an authoritative record for agents originating in Databricks — a system Zenity should know is in the customer's AI estate even where it has no direct integration. And the Anthropic connector tracking **per-user cost** means ServiceNow now holds per-individual usage data for a third-party AI platform, which is both a useful signal and a privacy-relevant data flow. The renaming of the Vertex connector is a small but real detection hazard: any Zenity logic matching that connector by name will miss it. Underneath all of them sits the concern flagged previously — each connector is a **standing set of cross-cloud credentials held inside the ServiceNow instance**, now with per-vendor authentication mechanisms worth evaluating individually (certificate-based for Microsoft, rotating keys for Amazon). AISPM should inventory configured connectors by version and vendor, match on identifiers rather than display names, resolve the identity and scope each authenticates with in the target cloud, and use the connector set to infer which AI platforms a customer runs

findings.title: Microsoft Foundry Notification Center aggregates Defender security alerts and guardrail policy violations into a portal-only feed
findings.description: Foundry has added a **Notification Center** that centralizes alerts for agents, models and projects into a single in-app feed, replacing what previously required manually configured Azure Monitor alerts across siloed systems. It covers four categories, two of which are security-relevant: **security alerts from Microsoft Defender for Cloud** — high-severity issues including malicious activity and **content safety violations** flagged against agents or their underlying infrastructure, surfaced through Azure's security alert APIs — and **policy and compliance notifications** from Azure Policy and **Foundry's built-in guardrails**, including ML governance policy violations. The rest are run completion and failure events for evaluations and training jobs. Zenity should care for two reasons. It is a **signal source**: guardrail violations and Defender detections against Foundry agents are exactly the events AIDR produces, so they should be correlated rather than duplicated, and the notification feed indicates what the platform itself already caught. And it is a **posture gap in its own right**: delivery is currently **portal-only in-app**, with no email or webhook channel documented, which means these security and compliance alerts are seen only by someone who logs into the Foundry portal and clicks the bell — high-severity Defender alerts about agents have no push path to a SOC. AISPM should record which Foundry projects have Defender for Cloud coverage and guardrail policies configured, and flag the absence of any external delivery channel for these alerts as an operational finding; AIDR should treat the alert categories as a correlation source

findings.title: Claude API responses now identify their originating workspace via the `anthropic-workspace-id` header
findings.description: Every Claude API response now carries an `anthropic-workspace-id` header holding the `wrkspc_`-prefixed ID of the workspace that the request's API key or access token resolved to, including the organization's Default Workspace. This is a small addition with real attribution value: workspaces are Anthropic's unit of spend, rate-limit and access segmentation, and until now the workspace behind a given key had to be looked up out-of-band or inferred. With the header, **every API response self-identifies its governance boundary**, which lets Zenity attribute observed traffic to a workspace directly from the response rather than maintaining a key-to-workspace mapping that drifts as keys are rotated or reassigned. The Default Workspace case is the useful signal: traffic resolving to the Default Workspace indicates a key that was never deliberately scoped to a purpose-built workspace, which is a reasonable posture finding on its own for organizations that have adopted workspace segmentation. AISPM should capture the header where it observes Claude API traffic, use it to build and continuously verify the key-to-workspace mapping, and flag production workloads resolving to the Default Workspace

findings.title: ChatGPT desktop app is now available on Linux, extending the endpoint agent surface to a third OS
findings.description: The ChatGPT desktop application entered preview for **Ubuntu, Debian and Fedora** on **x64 and ARM64**, distributed as `.deb` and `.rpm` packages. This is a straightforward but real expansion of ENDPOINT's scope: the same desktop agent Zenity tracks on macOS and Windows now runs on developer and server-adjacent Linux workstations, where endpoint agent tooling is typically thinnest and where package installation via `.deb`/`.rpm` may bypass the managed software channels used on the other two platforms. Detection logic, installation-path assumptions and configuration-file locations built for macOS and Windows will not carry over. Note the contrast with the Computer History finding above: that feature is macOS-only, so the Linux client has a different capability profile, and ENDPOINT should model per-OS feature availability rather than treating "ChatGPT desktop" as one uniform surface. ENDPOINT should add Linux package detection for the ChatGPT desktop app, establish its configuration and data paths, and extend existing macOS/Windows policy checks to the new platform
